# Jay L. Garfield & Graham Priest — "Nāgārjuna and the Limits of Thought" (2003)

## Source scholarship

The article's thesis is that Nāgārjuna "discovers and explores true contradictions arising at the limits of thought" — that the paradoxes of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* are not lapses or rhetorical devices but genuine dialetheias of the kind Priest's inclosure schema describes. The schema has three clauses: Existence (a totality Ω exists), Transcendence (the diagonalizer applied to any subset X yields something outside it, d(X) ∉ X), and Closure (that something nonetheless belongs to the totality, d(X) ∈ Ω); at the limit, applied to Ω itself, d(Ω) both is and is not in Ω. In Western logic the schema organizes Russell's paradox and the Gödelian limits; Garfield and Priest's claim is that Nāgārjuna's limit-contradictions have the same shape — which places him in the same formal genealogy the essay traces through Russell and Gödel in its formal-limit strand.

What they add is that Nāgārjuna's version is distinctively ontological. The contradiction is not about sets or sentences but about the nature of things: emptiness is the nature of all things, and that nature is precisely the lack of nature. They quote Nāgārjuna's autocommentary directly: "All things have one nature, that is, no nature." The paradox of expressibility follows the same fold, caught in the slogan they borrow from Siderits: "the ultimate truth is that there is no ultimate truth." On their reading none of this convicts Nāgārjuna of confusion; embracing the contradictions dialetheically "would not undermine, but instead would confirm, the impression that he [Nāgārjuna] is indeed a highly rational thinker" (close-verbatim) — the limits of thought are where a rigorous thinker ends up, not where a careless one falls.

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

The inclosure reading of Nāgārjuna: limit-contradictions with the Russell/Gödel shape, ontologized as emptiness — nature that is lack of nature — plus the Siderits slogan and the defense of Nāgārjuna's rationality.

### Licensed essay use

- Join Nāgārjuna to the essay's formal-limit genealogy in [[04-s01-p3-formal-limit-genealogy|04-s01-p3]], where the inclosure schema stands beside Russell and Gödel.
- Carry the ontological paradox (no-nature as nature) and the Siderits slogan into the §3 catuṣkoṭi reconstruction at [[28-s3-p3-projective-dimensional-reframing]].
- Use the rationality verdict to block deflationary readings of Nāgārjuna as mystic or sophist in the [[symbolon/episteme/histories/traditions-and-disciplines/indian-philosophy/HISTORY|indian-philosophy]] history strand.

### Claim boundary

The inclosure reading is one contested interpretation of Nāgārjuna, not the field's verdict; rival readings (including Siderits's own non-dialetheic semantic interpretation elsewhere) deny that any true contradiction is asserted. The essay may use the article as a serious formal reading with a live scholarly following; it may not present dialetheic Nāgārjuna as established. The mapping of the inclosure fold onto QL's ground/mark structure is the essay's own move.
